entities.name: Meissner effect
entities.label: EventWindow
entities.summary:
The Meissner effect is a phenomenon in which a superconductor expels a magnetic field during its transition to the superconducting state. This effect is named after the German physicist Walther Meissner, who first described it in 1933.

The Meissner effect is a fundamental property of superconductors and has been observed in a wide range of materials, including metals, alloys, and ceramic superconductors. It is a key characteristic of superconductivity and has been studied extensively in the fields of physics and materials science.

The Meissner effect has significant implications for the development of superconducting materials and devices, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines and high-energy particle accelerators. It has also led to a deeper understanding of the behavior of superconductors and their potential applications in fields such as energy and transportation.

One notable consequence of the Meissner effect is the development of high-temperature superconducting materials, which have the potential to revolutionize the way we transmit and store energy.
